演奏高腳鼓可夾於腋下，或坐姿時橫放腿上，鼓面朝向膝部；部分鼓有背帶，可掛肩站立或: The goblet drum can be tucked under the arm, or laid across the thighs when seated with the head towards the knees; some drums have a strap so that they can be slung on the shoulder while standing or dancing. It is sounded with light strokes of the fingertips and the palm: striking the centre of the head gives a low note, striking the rim gives a high one, and a stroke on the rim with the other hand gives a short, high note; briefly pressing the hand on the head gives a closed sound. A beginner practises the low, high and closed strokes first, then adds rolls, finger snaps, claps and strokes on the side of the shell. The Egyptian-style rim is rounded, which helps fast rolls; the Turkish type has an exposed rim, which makes snaps easier but fast rolls harder. The fist can also be moved in and out of the opening to change the timbre.

高腳鼓具有溫暖而富有穿透力的音色，兼具明亮與低沉的特質。敲擊鼓面中心產生深沉有力: The goblet drum has a warm, penetrating timbre that is at once bright and deep. Striking the centre of the head gives a deep, powerful low note like the weight of a bass drum; striking the rim gives a crisp, bright high note, a grace note at the edge. Its range is wide, from a full low register to a clear high one, and the sound is well layered. The resonance comes from the cup-shaped shell and produces a warm, resonant sound. Compared with the timpani the goblet drum has more local character and more flavour; compared with frame drums it is louder and fuller; compared with the snare drum it has a warmer finish. These sound characteristics make it important in the music of the Middle East and North Africa.
高腳鼓為單面膜鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號 211.26，常見: The goblet drum is a single-headed membranophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 211.26, common in the traditional music of North Africa, the Middle East and the Balkans and also found in South Asia and eastern Europe. West African goblet drums are several thousand years old and were used in Mesopotamian and ancient Egyptian culture; the earliest Babylonian and Sumerian examples go back to 1100 BC. The large goblet drums of Sulawesi serve as temple instruments and are placed on the ground to be played, which may reflect an ancient practice. The name 'darbuka' comes from Egyptian rural Arabic slang, from 'darb', to strike. From the nineteenth century the drum entered Western classical music: Hector Berlioz used a tarbuka in his opera Les Troyens, and in the mid-twentieth century Halim El-Dabh wrote a work for goblet drum and orchestra.
高腳鼓用於北非、中東與巴爾幹傳統音樂，亦見於南亞與東歐傳統音樂；蘇拉威西的大型高: The goblet drum is used in the traditional music of North Africa, the Middle East and the Balkans, and also in that of South Asia and eastern Europe; the large goblet drums of Sulawesi serve as temple instruments and are placed on the ground to be played. In Western classical scoring, Berlioz's opera Les Troyens uses a tarbuka in the 'Danse des esclaves nubiennes' in Act IV, and Halim El-Dabh's Fantasia-Tahmeel is written for goblet drum and string orchestra.
高腳鼓的鼓身採用陶土或金屬（如銅、鋁合金）製成，呈聖杯形。鼓面覆蓋動物皮革，傳統: The shell of the goblet drum is made of clay or metal such as copper or aluminium alloy and is shaped like a chalice. The head is covered with animal skin, traditionally often goatskin or fish skin, while modern instruments sometimes use a synthetic head. The hollow interior of the shell produces the resonance. The rim is usually reinforced with a metal ring, which helps with tuning. Goblet drums usually have tuning bolts or a rope-tension system to adjust the tension of the head and so the pitch.
高腳鼓（Goblet drum）是單面膜鳴樂器，鼓身高腳杯形，霍恩博斯特尔–薩克: The goblet drum is a single-headed membranophone with a goblet-shaped shell, Hornbostel–Sachs 211.26. Players usually tuck it under the arm or rest it on the legs and strike it lightly with the fingertips and the palm, which gives a resonant sound with a long decay; the fist can also be moved to change the timbre. It is common in the traditional music of North Africa, the Middle East, the Balkans, South Asia and eastern Europe, and the large goblet drums of Sulawesi serve as temple instruments.
